title: How large language models work
notes: A language model writes by predicting the next token, adding it and repeating; a token is about three quarters of a word.
The model sees only what is in its context window and keeps nothing between requests, so your code sends the whole conversation every time.
It sounds just as sure when it is wrong, so give it the facts and rules it needs instead of leaving gaps for it to fill.

slides.title: How large language models work
slides.sub: Tokens, prediction and the context window, and why a fluent answer can still be wrong
sentences: Welcome to Module 2, where you get to know the brain inside Scout.
In the hook, Scout promised Grace a ninety-day refund that Orbit has never offered.
To see why, you need to know how a language model actually produces text.
In about five minutes you will learn about tokens, how a reply gets written, what the model can see, and why it can be confidently wrong.

slides.title: One job: predict the next token

nodes.label: Next token
nodes.sub: one piece, added to the end

note.text: Then it runs again with the longer text. A 300-word reply is about 400 of these steps.

sentences: A large language model, or LLM, has one core job: given some text, predict what comes next.
It starts with your text, such as a customer asking where her order is.
That text is cut into small pieces called tokens.
The model reads all the tokens and gives every possible next token a score for how likely it is.
One token is chosen and added to the end of the text.
Then the whole thing runs again with the slightly longer text, until the reply is complete.
A three hundred word reply takes about four hundred of these steps.

slides.title: What is a token?
slides.definition: A small piece of text, often a whole word or part of one, that the model reads and writes.

parts.text: About three quarters of a word

analogy.label: Think of it as
analogy.text: Lego bricks: the model has a fixed box of pieces, and every reply is snapped together one brick at a time.

sentences: You will hear the word token constantly when you build with models, so let us pin it down.
Common words, like order or boots, are usually a single token.
Rare words, long product codes and many names are split into several pieces.
On average a token is about three quarters of a word, so a hundred words is roughly a hundred and thirty tokens.
Think of Lego bricks: the model has a fixed box of pieces, and every reply is snapped together one brick at a time.
Tokens matter to you because you pay per token, and a model's limits are counted in tokens too.

slides.title: How a reply gets written

center.label: Generation loop
center.sub: until an end token or your limit

note.text: Picking among likely tokens is called sampling. It is why wording varies from run to run.

sentences: Let us slow the loop down and watch one turn of it.
First, the model reads everything so far: your prompt, plus any part of the reply it has already written.
Next, it scores every token it knows, perhaps ninety percent for one word and tiny chances for thousands of others.
Then one token is picked, usually a very likely one, but not always the single top choice.
That token is added to the text, and the loop goes round again.
It stops when the model writes a special end token, or when it reaches the length limit you set.
Picking among likely options is called sampling, and it is why the same question can get differently worded answers.
That is normal, and it is one reason your code should never depend on exact wording.

slides.title: The context window: all the model can see

note.text: Not in the window? Then, as far as the model knows, it does not exist.

sentences: Everything the model can see during one request lives in its context window.
That includes the system prompt, where you give it a role, rules and facts.
It includes the conversation so far, every message from the customer and from Scout.
From Module 3 on, it will include tool results too, such as an order your code looked up.
And the reply it is writing counts as well, token by token.
The models in this course can hold up to a million tokens, which is several long novels.
But the model keeps nothing between requests: whatever is not in the window, it cannot see.
That is exactly why your chatbot in Module 1 kept a list of messages and sent the whole list every turn.

slides.title: What it learned versus what you must tell it

left.label: Learned in training
points: Broad facts, up to a cutoff date
Common patterns, like typical return windows

sentences: So where does the model's knowledge come from?
During training, it read a vast amount of text and learned how language works, along with a lot of general knowledge.
That learning stopped at a cutoff date, and chatting with it does not teach it anything new.
It also learned common patterns, such as many shops offering thirty, sixty or ninety day returns.
What it never saw is anything private to Orbit.
It does not know Orbit's policy, Grace's order, or where a parcel is today.
The only way it can use those facts is if you put them into its context window.

slides.title: Sure, fluent and wrong

messages.label: Grace
messages.text: Hi! Can I still return my Ridge boots? They arrived about two months ago.

messages.label: Scout · no policy
messages.text: Absolutely, we offer 90-day refunds! You're well within the window.

messages.label: Added to the system prompt
messages.text: Returns: unused items within 30 days of delivery. Never promise what the policy doesn't say.

messages.label: Scout · policy in context
messages.text: Sorry, Grace. Returns are accepted within 30 days of delivery, so boots from two months ago are outside the window. I can ask the team if anything else is possible.

aside.label: Hallucination
aside.text: A fluent, confident answer that is not true. The model filled a gap with something likely.

sentences: Now you can see what went wrong in the hook.
Grace asked whether she could return boots that arrived two months ago.
Scout had no policy in its context, so it predicted the most plausible reply, and ninety-day refunds sounded plausible.
This is called a hallucination: a fluent, confident answer that is simply not true.
The model sounds just as sure when it is wrong as when it is right, because it is predicting text, not checking facts.
So we add the real policy, and one rule, to the system prompt.
Now the same model gives Grace the honest answer, and offers a next step it can actually keep.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: An LLM writes by predicting the next token, again and again
A token is about three quarters of a word, and you pay per token
It sees only its context window and keeps nothing between requests
It sounds just as sure when wrong: give it the facts and the rules

sentences: Let us pull it together.
A language model writes by predicting the next token, again and again.
A token is about three quarters of a word, and tokens are what you pay for.
The model only sees what is in its context window, and it keeps nothing between requests.
It sounds just as sure when it is wrong, so give it the facts and the rules it needs.
Next, you will choose which model Scout should use, and look closely at a request and its response.

midQuiz.q: A customer email is about 300 words long. Roughly how many tokens is that?
midQuiz.explain: A token is about three quarters of a word, so 300 words is roughly 400 tokens.
midQuiz.hint: Each token is a bit less than a whole word, so expect a few more tokens than words.

midQuiz.q: You ask Scout the same question twice and get two differently worded answers. Why?
options: Something is broken and needs fixing
Sampling: it picks among likely tokens, not always the top one
The context window was full the second time
midQuiz.explain: Each step picks from the likely next tokens, so the wording varies between runs. That is normal.
midQuiz.hint: Think about the Pick step in the generation loop.

endQuiz.q: Why did Scout promise Grace a 90-day refund?
options: It read an old version of Orbit's policy
No policy was in its context, so it predicted a plausible answer
Grace's email told it to say 90 days
endQuiz.explain: The model only sees its context. With no policy and no rule, it filled the gap with a common, plausible answer.
endQuiz.hint: What was actually in the context window when Scout wrote the reply?

endQuiz.q: In a chat, Scout answers the third message as if the first two never happened. What is the most likely cause?
options: The context window only holds one message
Your code sent only the newest message, not the whole conversation
The model's training cutoff is too old
endQuiz.explain: The model keeps nothing between requests, so your code must send the whole conversation every time.
endQuiz.hint: Between requests, where does the conversation live: in the model, or in your code?
